## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with substantial morbidity, including stroke, heart failure, hospitalization, and reduced quality of life. Atrial fibrillation results from disorganized atrial electrical activity that produces an irregular ventricular rhythm and may cause a rapid ventricular response. The pulmonary veins are important sources of atrial fibrillation triggers, particularly in paroxysmal disease, while progressive electrical and structural remodeling can promote persistence and progression of the arrhythmia.

Atrial fibrillation is promoted by a complex interaction of electrical, structural, and clinical factors. Hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, heart failure, coronary artery disease, sleep-disordered breathing, alcohol consumption, and advancing age are among the important risk factors associated with its development and progression. Loss of effective atrial contraction and irregular ventricular activation can impair cardiac function, while blood stasis, particularly in the left atrial appendage, promotes thrombus formation and increases the risk of systemic thromboembolism and ischemic stroke.

For this reason, evaluation and management of atrial fibrillation require assessment of the arrhythmia itself as well as associated cardiovascular disease, thromboembolic risk, modifiable risk factors, symptoms, and patient-specific treatment goals. Current management emphasizes comprehensive risk-factor modification, stroke prevention, and individualized rate- or rhythm-control strategies, with catheter ablation increasingly used earlier in selected patients.

## Etiology

Atrial fibrillation is a multifactorial arrhythmia associated with cardiovascular disease, systemic conditions, and modifiable risk factors. Common causes and contributing conditions include:

Advanced age

Hypertension

Coronary artery disease and other structural heart disease

Valvular heart disease, particularly mitral valve disease

Heart failure and left ventricular dysfunction

Congenital heart disease

Increased alcohol consumption

Obesity

Obstructive sleep apnea

Diabetes mellitus

Hyperthyroidism and other endocrine disorders

Genetic predisposition

Myocarditis and pericarditis

Pulmonary embolism and other conditions associated with hemodynamic stress

Neurologic disorders, including stroke and subarachnoid hemorrhage

Iatrogenic causes, including cardiac surgery and other cardiac procedures

Any condition that causes atrial stretch, inflammation, ischemia, fibrosis, or electrical remodeling can contribute to the development or progression of atrial fibrillation. In some patients, no single underlying cause is identified.

## Pathophysiology

Atrial fibrillation develops through a complex interaction of electrical triggers, atrial substrate, and structural and electrical remodeling. Structural remodeling includes atrial dilation, myocyte changes, extracellular matrix alterations, and interstitial fibrosis, which disrupt normal electrical conduction and promote persistence of the arrhythmia. Electrical remodeling includes changes in ion-channel function, shortened atrial refractory periods, and altered conduction that increase susceptibility to recurrent atrial fibrillation. Tachycardia itself can further promote electrical and structural remodeling, creating a self-perpetuating cycle.[PMID: 41543444; PMID: 21248168]

Most cases of atrial fibrillation are associated with acquired cardiovascular or systemic conditions rather than a single genetic abnormality. Hypertension, heart failure, valvular disease, coronary artery disease, obesity, sleep-disordered breathing, aging, and other conditions that promote atrial stretch, inflammation, ischemia, or fibrosis contribute to the development of an atrial substrate capable of sustaining fibrillation. Genetic factors also contribute to susceptibility, although monogenic causes account for a minority of cases.[PMID: 38043043; PMID: 34113869]

Atrial fibrillation is commonly initiated by ectopic electrical activity arising from the pulmonary veins, particularly at the pulmonary vein–left atrial junction. Once initiated, reentrant electrical activity and abnormal conduction can propagate through atrial tissue with altered refractory periods, resulting in rapid, uncoordinated atrial activation. Loss of effective atrial contraction and irregular ventricular activation can reduce cardiac efficiency, while blood stasis, particularly within the left atrial appendage, promotes thrombus formation and increases the risk of thromboembolic events.[PMID: 41543444; PMID: 32717172; PMID: 33252128]

Important mechanisms and triggers associated with atrial fibrillation include:

Atrial stretch and hemodynamic stress

Atrial ischemia

Inflammation and fibrosis

Alcohol and stimulant or illicit drug exposure

Autonomic nervous system influences

Endocrine disorders, particularly hyperthyroidism

Aging

Genetic susceptibility

Structural and valvular heart disease

Heart failure[PMID: 34113869; PMID: 41543444]

## History and Physical

History and physical examination are essential for recognizing atrial fibrillation, identifying potential precipitants and underlying conditions, assessing symptom burden, and determining hemodynamic stability. Clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic disease to hemodynamic compromise and thromboembolic complications. Patients may report palpitations, fatigue, chest discomfort, dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, dizziness, or peripheral edema. The history should establish the duration, frequency, and pattern of symptoms; potential precipitants; previous episodes and methods of termination; prior antiarrhythmic or rate-control therapy; and relevant cardiac history.

The medical history should assess conditions and exposures associated with atrial fibrillation, including hypertension, structural or ischemic heart disease, valvular disease, heart failure, sleep-disordered breathing, obesity, diabetes mellitus, thyroid disease, alcohol consumption, smoking, stimulant or illicit drug use, and previous cardiac or inflammatory disease. Patients should also be assessed for symptoms or risk factors suggesting stroke, heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, or other conditions that may contribute to or mimic atrial fibrillation.

The initial assessment should determine whether the patient is hemodynamically stable. Physical examination may reveal an irregularly irregular pulse and tachycardia, although ventricular rate may be normal or slow. The cardiovascular examination should assess for murmurs and other findings suggesting structural or valvular heart disease. Pulmonary examination may identify pulmonary congestion or other underlying pulmonary disease. Assessment for peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, or other signs of heart failure is appropriate when clinically indicated.

A focused neurologic examination is important when symptoms or clinical findings raise concern for stroke or transient ischemic attack. The examination should also be directed toward identifying potential contributors or complications rather than routinely performing extensive vascular, abdominal, or neurologic examinations in every patient.
